d0a311081328f2e0a769614c57c594afb47337f7.summary: JFrog Security Research describes the 'testmetest' campaign: an npm worm and a hidden CI publisher that armed 42 GitHub repositories across 11 owners, including accounts of real developers and organizations. It uses a native addon that decrypts a hidden file at runtime, forged commit dates, and execution hooks for AI coding assistants and IDEs. The report links this infrastructure to shellpanel scanning of cPanel systems via CVE-2026-41940, but says downstream compromises are not confirmed. Attribution to the original Miasma operators is not established.

Initial access came through a compromised third-party vendor. The attacker spent weeks moving laterally with Cobalt Strike and tunnelling tools, exfiltrated data with Rclone to cloud storage, and sent extortion emails. The client blocked internet access, which stopped encryption. Stolen files were later published on the group's leak site.

d0d666177b14b04a9202863e5b062a0e5936b161.summary: AhnLab's ASEC analysis team reports signs of AppleSeed malware being spread to maintenance contractors of a military unit, in July 2022. hedges: It should be noted that many of the low-level technical details of the startup process are beyond the scope of this paper.
The attribution of the CallMe targeting to the Chinese government is marked 'likely' by the paper.
The paper says the description of OSX/Crisis as an expensive rootkit used by governments comes from online sources.
The paper says Janicab is probably signed with an Apple Developer ID in an attempt to hide its maliciousness and thwart Gatekeeper.
The paper says older persistence methods are likely to fade into oblivion because they no longer work on the latest OS X.
The paper notes that the KnockKnock approach will also list legitimate binaries, which can be filtered.
The paper says Clapzok will likely cause major annoyances and will be easily discovered.
The paper notes that not all persistence methods presented are (yet) abused by OS X malware.
